name: Raleigh
title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Raleigh, NC | Genstone
metaDescription: Raleigh, NC renovation contractor for investors: Beltline ranches, Oakwood-era houses and North Raleigh split-levels, scoped before you make the offer.
intro: Inside Raleigh's Beltline, an older house competes with builders who would happily tear it down, so a renovation has to beat the value of the dirt underneath it. Outside the Beltline, the numbers look more like a classic rental or flip market, built on post-war ranches, 1970s and 1980s split-levels and townhomes that were never updated. Genstone Construction renovates for investors, lenders and servicers across Wake County, from Southeast Raleigh to the North Raleigh subdivisions and out to Garner, Knightdale and Wake Forest. Genstone is based in Romeoville, Illinois, without a Raleigh branch. Here we coordinate vetted, licensed Triangle contractors under one designated field manager who handles permits with City of Raleigh Development Services, inspections and lien waivers. Every project begins with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review that estimates repairs and refines the after-repair value before you commit, and continues with a line-item scope, a draw schedule paid against finished work, and final billing only after you approve the house.
housingStock:
Raleigh's oldest residential fabric sits in a ring around downtown. Oakwood has the city's largest concentration of Victorian-era houses, including Queen Anne and Second Empire homes with tall ceilings, heavy millwork and balloon framing. Mordecai, Glenwood-Brooklyn and Boylan Heights carry early twentieth-century bungalows, foursquares and cottages, typically on brick foundations with crawlspaces and, on sloping lots, partial basements. Five Points and Hayes Barton add 1920s and 1930s Tudor and Colonial Revival houses with plaster walls, steam or converted heating systems and the occasional slate or clay tile roof.

After World War II the city spread quickly. Brentwood, Longview Gardens, the streets off Glenwood Avenue near North Hills and much of the area inside and just outside the Beltline filled with brick and frame ranches, many with hardwood floors, single-bath layouts and small kitchens. Southeast Raleigh around Biltmore Hills, Worthdale and Rochester Heights has similar ranch stock plus some earlier frame cottages. In the 1970s and 1980s North Raleigh exploded with split-levels, contemporaries with cathedral ceilings, and large numbers of townhomes. The 1990s and 2000s brought big subdivisions near Brier Creek, Wakefield and the eastern edge toward Knightdale.

Each generation shows up in an estimate differently. Victorian and bungalow work is dominated by framing corrections, plaster versus drywall decisions, wiring replacement and historic district rules. Ranches need kitchens, baths, crawlspace work and electrical capacity. North Raleigh's 1970s and 1980s houses often hide the most surprising costs: hardboard siding that has swollen at the drip edge, aluminum branch wiring in some late-1960s and early-1970s builds, polybutylene plumbing, and decks and windows built with materials that didn't last. The 1990s and 2000s subdivisions are simpler to read: original roofs, heat pumps, water heaters and builder-grade carpet tend to reach the end of their lives together, so the budget is predictable even when it isn't small.

commonIssues.title: Hardboard siding failures
commonIssues.body: Many North Raleigh and Cary-area houses from the 1980s and 1990s were clad in pressed hardboard siding that swells, softens and grows mold when water gets past the paint, usually along bottom edges, near gutters and behind shrubs. Buyers' inspectors know exactly what it looks like. Patching individual boards rarely holds, so the estimate should compare targeted replacement on the worst elevations against a full re-side in fiber cement, with new house wrap and flashing at windows and doors.

commonIssues.title: Aluminum branch wiring and older panels
commonIssues.body: Some houses wired in the late 1960s and early 1970s, a period well represented in Raleigh's outer neighborhoods, used aluminum branch circuit wiring, which loosens at connections and can overheat. Insurers and inspectors flag it. Remediation with approved connectors at every device, or rewiring where walls are open, should be scoped up front. The same era brought panels from manufacturers that home inspectors routinely recommend replacing, so the electrical line on a Raleigh estimate often grows quickly.

commonIssues.title: Crawlspace and grading moisture
commonIssues.body: Raleigh sits on Piedmont soils that shed water slowly, and many inside-the-Beltline houses were built with little attention to grading. Water collects against foundations, finds its way into crawlspaces and partial basements, and leaves rotted sill plates, rusty ductwork and musty interiors behind. The fix is almost always a combination of exterior grading, gutters and downspout extensions, a proper vapor barrier and, when the exit strategy supports it, a conditioned or encapsulated crawlspace.

commonIssues.title: Trees over the roof
commonIssues.body: Mature pines and hardwoods are part of Raleigh's appeal, and they are also a constant roofing and gutter problem. Pine needles clog valleys and gutters, overhanging limbs scrape shingles, and in storms like Hurricane Fran in 1996 whole trees landed on houses across the city. A rehab scope here should include an arborist's look at large trees near the house, roof and gutter repair caused by debris, and sometimes removal before the roof goes on.

commonIssues.title: Plaster, lead and asbestos in older houses
commonIssues.body: Oakwood, Mordecai and Five Points houses usually have original plaster over wood lath, layers of lead paint on trim and windows, and in some cases asbestos in old boiler insulation, pipe wrap or flooring. Removing plaster creates heavy debris and dust, and disturbing painted surfaces requires lead-safe practices from an RRP-certified firm. We test before demolition and decide room by room whether to repair plaster or replace it, since the cost and schedule differ significantly.

investorMarket:
Raleigh's investor activity splits along the Beltline. Inside it, neighborhoods like Five Points, Mordecai and parts of Oakwood are among the most expensive in the region, and many smaller houses are bought by builders for new construction. A flip there has to deliver a finished product that justifies paying more than land value, which usually means a substantial renovation, sometimes with an addition. East College Park, Longview Gardens, South Park and the area around Oberlin are earlier in their transition, and older ranches and cottages there still trade at prices that leave room for a full rehab.

Outside the Beltline, Southeast Raleigh's ranch neighborhoods, the older parts of North Raleigh and the townhome communities along Capital Boulevard and Spring Forest Road attract rental and BRRRR investors. Further out, Garner, Knightdale, Wendell and Zebulon have newer stock with steady renter demand from people working across the Triangle. Near NC State, student rental demand supports duplexes and small apartment buildings around Avent Ferry Road and Method.

Raleigh's missing middle zoning changes in 2021 and 2022 allowed duplexes, triplexes, townhouses and backyard cottages on many residential lots that used to be single-family only. That has changed the math on larger lots inside the Beltline, where adding a unit can sometimes beat a straight flip.
permits:
City of Raleigh Development Services issues building and trade permits and performs inspections for addresses inside the city limits. Properties in unincorporated Wake County go through Wake County Permit and Inspections, and towns like Cary, Garner and Knightdale run their own departments. In Raleigh, structural changes, additions, new or relocated plumbing and electrical circuits, HVAC replacements, water heaters and decks all require permits, while painting, flooring, cabinets and replacing fixtures in the same location generally don't. Licensed trade contractors pull their own permits, and inspections follow footing, rough-in, insulation and final stages.

Raleigh's Historic Overlay Districts, including Oakwood, Boylan Heights and Glenwood-Brooklyn, require a Certificate of Appropriateness from the Raleigh Historic Development Commission for exterior changes visible from the street. Window replacement, porch reconstruction, siding changes, roofing materials and additions are reviewed, and minor works can often be approved by staff while larger changes go to the commission. Genstone's field manager prepares and tracks the applications, schedules inspections with Development Services and collects lien waivers from every trade.
climate: Raleigh's climate is humid subtropical, with hot, sticky summers that load air conditioners and crawlspaces with moisture, and mild winters punctuated by the occasional ice storm. Ice is more dangerous to houses here than snow: the December 2002 ice storm left much of the Triangle without power and dropped limbs on roofs across the city. Tropical systems arrive every few years with heavy rain and wind, and Raleigh's tall pines make wind events a roofing problem as much as a weather problem. Summer thunderstorms test gutters, grading and window flashing. For scheduling, roofing, siding and exterior paint move most smoothly in spring and fall, while interior work fits any season. We also plan for pollen season in spring, when the yellow coating on everything can interfere with exterior painting.

faqs.q: Does Genstone renovate houses inside the Beltline?
faqs.a: Yes. Inside-the-Beltline projects tend to be larger renovations where the finished house has to compete with new construction on nearby lots, and they often involve historic district review in Oakwood, Boylan Heights or Glenwood-Brooklyn. We coordinate licensed local contractors who work on older Raleigh houses and assign a field manager to handle the Raleigh Historic Development Commission process, permits with Development Services and the line-item budget.

faqs.q: Do you work in Cary, Garner and the other Wake County towns?
faqs.a: Yes. Our Raleigh-area work covers Wake County generally, including Cary, Garner, Knightdale, Wake Forest, Apex, Holly Springs and Wendell. Each town has its own building and inspections department and its own zoning rules, so permits and inspections run through the jurisdiction where the property sits. The process on our side is the same everywhere: free Pre-Offer Rehab Review, line-item estimate, designated field manager, draws tied to completed work.

faqs.q: What does a Raleigh Pre-Offer Rehab Review look for?
faqs.a: On a Raleigh house we pay close attention to the items that drive budgets here: hardboard siding condition, aluminum wiring or problem panels, polybutylene supply lines, crawlspace moisture and framing, roof age and tree risk, and whether the property is in a Historic Overlay District. We estimate the repair cost, check the after-repair value against recent sales nearby and tell you whether the numbers support your offer before your capital is committed.

faqs.q: How does Genstone get paid on a Raleigh project?
faqs.a: There's no upfront payment. Your estimate includes a draw schedule, and each draw is tied to work that has been completed and documented with photos and, where relevant, passed inspections. Final payment follows completion and your approval. Dumpster and debris costs are already in the estimate. After completion, a one-year workmanship warranty covers our work, though tenant damage and normal wear are excluded.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Raleigh, NC | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Fix and flip contractor in Raleigh, NC: renovations that compete with Beltline new construction and sell in Southeast and North Raleigh, managed end to end.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Raleigh
fix-flip.intro: The hardest competitor for a Raleigh flip is often a new house going up two lots down. Inside the Beltline, buyers can choose between your renovated 1950s ranch and a builder's new two-story, and the renovation has to win on layout, finish and condition. Outside the Beltline, the competition is other flips, and speed and clean inspections matter more than custom finishes. Genstone Construction builds Raleigh flip scopes around which of those markets your house is in. Our estimators price the work line by line, often with more than one finish level tied to different after-repair values, and a designated field manager runs the job with licensed local trades, permits through City of Raleigh Development Services and documentation you can follow from anywhere.

sections.h2: Flipping inside the Beltline versus outside it
sections.body:
In Five Points, Mordecai, Hayes Barton or the Glenwood corridor near North Hills, the buyer has typically toured new construction and expects similar functionality: an open kitchen with an island, a primary suite with a real bathroom, plenty of storage and a finished outdoor space. Older houses there often need an addition, a reworked floor plan or a second bath carved out of a bedroom to compete. The finish level has to be genuinely high, and the house needs to look intentional rather than flipped. Historic district rules can apply to exterior changes.

Outside the Beltline in Southeast Raleigh, Longview Gardens, North Raleigh or Garner, flips usually sell to owner-occupants using conventional or FHA loans, and appraisals depend on nearby sales. A clean, durable renovation with new mechanicals, good flooring, a functional kitchen and refreshed baths is what moves. Spending for designer features on those streets often isn't recovered. Our estimates show the cost of each level so you can choose the scope that matches where the house actually sits.

sections.h2: North Raleigh split-levels and the inspection report
sections.body:
The 1970s and 1980s houses of North Raleigh look like easy flips and often aren't. Split-levels and contemporaries off Six Forks Road, Falls of Neuse and Spring Forest Road were built quickly with materials that age poorly, and the buyer's inspector will find them. Hardboard siding with swollen bottom edges, aluminum branch wiring in some of the earliest builds, polybutylene supply lines, rotted deck ledgers attached without flashing, single-pane or failing early double-pane windows and skylights that leak are all common.

We scope those items up front rather than discovering them under contract. That might mean replacing siding on the weather-facing elevations, remediating wiring, repiping in PEX, rebuilding the deck to current code and sealing or removing skylights. Those aren't the photogenic parts of a flip, but they decide whether the sale closes at your price. Permits and final inspections for that work are part of the package we hand your listing agent, and they answer the inspector's questions before they're asked.

sections.h2: Managing schedule and cost on a Raleigh flip
sections.body:
Holding costs on Raleigh flips include interest, insurance, utilities and property taxes, and a project inside the Beltline at a higher purchase price feels every extra month. We shorten the critical path by finalizing the scope before closing, submitting permits to Development Services or the Historic Development Commission immediately, and ordering windows, cabinets and specialty items during review instead of after demolition. Trades are scheduled so rough-in inspections are grouped, and exterior work is timed around Raleigh's spring pollen and summer storms.

Draws follow completed work, never ahead of it. The field manager documents progress with photos and milestones, which matters for investors who don't live in the Triangle and lenders who need verification before releasing funds. If you want construction lending coordinated in-house, Genstone Financial offers fix-and-flip loans and lines of credit, but we work with any lender. Dumpster and debris costs are already in the estimate, so a gut renovation doesn't generate a surprise invoice at the halfway point.

faqs.q: Is it worth flipping a small house inside the Raleigh Beltline?
faqs.a: Sometimes. When builders are paying close to the purchase price for the lot, a flip only works if the renovated house sells for meaningfully more than the land plus your total cost. That usually means a substantial renovation or an addition. During the Pre-Offer Rehab Review we can price the renovation and compare the resulting ARV with recent new construction and lot sales, so you can see whether a flip, a wholesale to a builder or an added unit makes the most sense.

faqs.q: Can I replace windows on a flip in Oakwood or Boylan Heights?
faqs.a: Possibly, but it requires a Certificate of Appropriateness from the Raleigh Historic Development Commission, and the commission generally favors repairing original wood windows over replacing them with vinyl. Repair and storm windows are often approved more readily. We plan window work around the district guidelines and build the review time into the flip schedule so you aren't waiting on an approval with the house half finished.

faqs.q: Which flips tend to move quickly in Raleigh?
faqs.a: We won't predict a sale, but the pattern we see is consistent: houses with clean inspections, updated mechanicals and a floor plan that works for how people live now tend to move, while houses with obvious deferred items or awkward layouts sit. In Raleigh that often means fixing siding and wiring issues on 1980s houses, and opening up closed kitchens in ranches. Your listing agent's read on the neighborhood is the most useful guide to finishes.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Raleigh, NC | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: BRRRR renovations in Raleigh, NC for rental investors: ranches, split-levels and townhomes rehabbed to appraise and rent, with draws and full documentation.
brrrr.intro: Raleigh's steady job growth has made it a reliable rental market, which is why so many BRRRR investors focus on the ranches of Southeast Raleigh, the townhomes of North Raleigh and the newer stock in Garner and Knightdale. In Wake County, the hard part is the purchase price. Purchase prices across Wake County leave less room than they used to, so the renovation has to be efficient and the appraisal has to land where you need it. Genstone Construction scopes BRRRR projects to add value where Raleigh appraisers recognize it, using materials that hold up to tenants. A designated field manager runs the work, every repair is documented for your refinance lender, and draws are paid only for completed work.

sections.h2: Choosing Raleigh properties that support the refinance
sections.body:
A BRRRR in Raleigh starts with buying a house whose renovated value clearly exceeds your all-in cost. That usually points to properties with deferred maintenance or dated interiors that scare off retail buyers, like a ranch in Biltmore Hills or Rochester Heights with an original kitchen and a failing roof, a North Raleigh split-level with siding damage and old wiring, or a townhome off Spring Forest Road that hasn't been touched in decades.

The Pre-Offer Rehab Review helps you separate the good candidates from the money pits. We estimate the cost of bringing the house to rental-ready, appraisal-ready condition, look at what renovated comparable houses nearby have sold for, and tell you whether the gap supports a refinance. Townhomes deserve a special note: HOA rules may control exterior materials, roofing and even window styles, and some associations restrict rentals, so we review the HOA documents before scoping exterior work. A house that only pencils with an exterior overhaul the association won't allow is better passed over.

sections.h2: What a Raleigh refinance appraiser wants to see
sections.body:
Appraisers in Wake County look at condition and quality ratings as well as comparable sales. A rental that has a fully updated kitchen, renovated bathrooms, new flooring, fresh paint and visibly new mechanicals earns a better condition rating than one with a partial update. Unresolved items like a stained ceiling from an old roof leak, a soft spot in the bathroom floor or swollen siding near the back door can pull the rating down even if the rest of the house is finished.

We close those gaps before the appraiser walks in. On Raleigh's older ranches, that often means replacing the HVAC system and ductwork, upgrading the panel, refinishing hardwood and installing a new roof. On 1980s houses it means siding, windows and deck repairs. We provide an improvement summary with permit records, final inspections and before-and-after photos, which gives the appraiser documented evidence of the work instead of a guess based on the walk-through.

sections.h2: Materials for a Raleigh rental that lasts
sections.body:
Rental durability in Raleigh comes down to moisture, heat and tenant wear. We favor fiber cement over hardboard when siding needs replacement, since it won't swell when it gets wet. Inside, luxury vinyl plank stands up to moisture and pets, and we refinish existing hardwood in ranches where it's sound. Bathrooms get exterior-vented fans with timers or humidity controls, and kitchens get durable counters and cabinets that can take years of use.

Mechanicals matter most for long-term rentals here. A properly sized heat pump with sealed ducts handles Raleigh's long cooling season without constant service calls. PEX supply lines replace polybutylene or galvanized pipe, and a new water heater with a drain pan protects the floor framing. Crawlspace vapor barriers and gutters with downspout extensions reduce the moisture that leads to mold complaints. These choices keep your maintenance costs predictable after the refinance, and they're the same items that make the property easier to sell later.

faqs.q: Are townhomes good BRRRR properties in Raleigh?
faqs.a: They can be, especially the older North Raleigh communities where purchase prices leave room for renovation. The trade-offs are HOA dues, which affect DSCR calculations, and HOA rules that may limit rentals or control exterior changes. We review the HOA documents during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review and focus the scope on interior work and mechanicals, which are usually the owner's responsibility in Raleigh townhome communities.

faqs.q: Can I BRRRR near NC State?
faqs.a: Yes, and student demand around Avent Ferry Road, Method and the Western Boulevard corridor is steady. Student rentals need tougher materials and more bedrooms, and some lenders view them differently for DSCR purposes. Raleigh also limits the number of unrelated people who can live together in a single-family dwelling, so check the zoning and occupancy rules before planning bedroom additions.

faqs.q: Does Genstone offer refinance loans?
faqs.a: Genstone Financial, part of the Genstone Companies, offers DSCR rental loans for the refinance stage, plus fix-and-flip loans and lines of credit for acquisition and renovation. You can use them or any other lender. Either way, we provide the itemized scope, permit and inspection records and photo documentation that Raleigh lenders and appraisers typically ask for at the refinance, organized so the file is easy to review.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Raleigh, NC | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Rental property renovation in Raleigh and Wake County, NC: single-family and townhome rehabs, turns and deferred maintenance for investors and SFR portfolios.
rental-renovation.intro: Wake County has drawn a large share of the single-family rental investment in North Carolina, and Raleigh rentals range from 1950s ranches near downtown to townhomes in North Raleigh and newer houses in Garner, Knightdale and Wake Forest. Genstone Construction renovates those properties for individual landlords, funds, REITs and other portfolio owners. We handle acquisition rehabs that bring a property to rent-ready condition, turns between tenants and the deferred maintenance projects that build up in a portfolio over time. Each job gets a designated field manager, licensed local trades and documentation you can review without visiting the house. When you own more than one Raleigh rental, we can standardize materials and scopes across the portfolio.

sections.h2: Rent-ready standards across Raleigh's housing types
sections.body:
A portfolio in the Raleigh area often mixes very different properties. A brick ranch in Southeast Raleigh needs crawlspace, electrical and plumbing attention. A 1980s townhome needs siding, windows and interior updates within whatever the HOA allows. A 2000s house in Knightdale or Wendell usually needs roof, HVAC and water heater replacements as original equipment ages out. Treating them all the same wastes money on some and underserves others.

We create a portfolio specification that keeps the visible items consistent, including flooring, paint colors, fixtures, appliances and hardware, so your property manager stocks fewer parts and tenants get a predictable experience. Then each property gets an era-specific scope based on what tends to fail in that type of house. At the end of each project, we record system ages and equipment details so future capital planning is based on actual data rather than assumptions. When three houses in the same Knightdale subdivision all have original heat pumps, for example, you can budget the replacements in one year instead of reacting to three emergency calls.

sections.h2: Reducing work orders in Raleigh rentals
sections.body:
The most common Raleigh rental work orders trace back to a few sources: HVAC systems working hard through long, humid summers, clogged gutters under heavy tree cover, bathroom moisture and plumbing leaks. A rental renovation that addresses those sources pays back through fewer calls and shorter turns.

We size heat pumps properly and seal ductwork, especially in crawlspaces where leaky ducts pull in humid air. We add gutter guards or schedule cleanings where pines drop needles, and we make sure downspouts discharge away from foundations. Bathrooms get fans that vent outside and tile or one-piece surrounds that don't leak at seams. Supply lines move to PEX, and water heaters get pans and proper drains. On the finish side, durable flooring and scrubbable paint survive move-outs. None of these items change the rent on their own, but together they change what the property costs to own. They also make the house easier to keep leased, because Raleigh renters have plenty of newer options and remember a summer with a broken air conditioner.

sections.h2: Turns and make-ready for Raleigh rentals
sections.body:
Turn speed is where rental profits are kept or lost. Genstone Construction handles make-ready work across the Raleigh area, and Genstone Field Services supports portfolio owners with inspections, occupied maintenance, turns and code compliance. A turn typically includes paint, flooring repair or replacement, fixture checks, appliance testing, cleaning and repair of damage left by the previous tenant.

We photograph the property at the start of the turn so your property manager has documentation for deposit decisions. If the turn reveals a bigger problem, like a slow leak under a sink that has softened the cabinet floor or swollen siding that has let water into a wall, we document it and price it separately so you can decide whether to address it now or put it on next year's capital list. Draws are tied to completed work, and the one-year workmanship warranty covers our repairs, though tenant damage and normal wear are not included.

faqs.q: Do you handle rental renovations for funds and REITs in Raleigh?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone works with individual investors as well as investment funds, REITs, mortgage servicers and banks. For portfolio owners in the Raleigh area we can apply consistent specifications across properties, provide standardized reporting and assign field managers who understand the reporting requirements of institutional owners. Each property still has its own scope, budget, schedule and documentation, so a single house can be reviewed on its own.

faqs.q: Can you renovate rentals in Raleigh HOA communities?
faqs.a: Yes. Many Raleigh rentals are in townhome or subdivision HOAs that control exterior changes, require approval for roofing or siding colors and sometimes limit work hours. We review the HOA rules and submit any required architectural review applications before starting exterior work, and we coordinate access to shared areas with the management company when needed. Interior renovations rarely need association approval, so they can usually start while any exterior application is under review.

faqs.q: How do you price Raleigh rental turns?
faqs.a: We walk or review the property, document conditions with photos and price each repair line by line. For portfolio clients we can set standard pricing for common turn items so approvals move quickly. Anything outside the standard scope is priced separately and approved before work begins. Dumpster and debris removal are included, and no payment is due until the work is complete.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex and 2–4 Unit Renovation in Raleigh, NC | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Duplex, triplex and fourplex renovation in Raleigh, NC: student-area quads, older east Raleigh duplexes and missing-middle conversions, phased around tenants.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Duplex and Small Multifamily Renovation in Raleigh
multifamily-renovation.intro: Raleigh's small multifamily stock comes from three directions. Near NC State, duplexes and quadplexes from the 1970s and 1980s were built for students and have housed them ever since. In the older neighborhoods east and south of downtown, some large houses were divided into apartments decades ago. And since the city's missing middle zoning changes, investors can add units to many lots that used to allow only one house, which has pulled new buyers into the small multifamily market. Genstone Construction renovates two- to four-unit buildings in Raleigh for investors who need shared systems upgraded, units modernized, tenants managed during construction and permits handled correctly. A designated field manager coordinates licensed local trades, and every draw follows completed work.

sections.h2: Renovating Raleigh's student-area duplexes and quads
sections.body:
The duplexes and quadplexes around Avent Ferry Road, Gorman Street and the Western Boulevard corridor were built for durability on a budget, and decades of student tenants have tested them. Typical issues include worn-out flooring, damaged doors and drywall, original or early replacement windows, aging HVAC systems in every unit and plumbing that's been patched repeatedly. Exterior stairs and balconies on two-story buildings are a frequent concern, since wood framing exposed to Raleigh's humidity and summer storms rots at connections.

We renovate those buildings to handle the same use for years to come. That means luxury vinyl plank or sealed concrete instead of carpet, solid-core doors, impact-resistant wall finishes in hallways, durable cabinets and counters, and new heat pumps sized for each unit. Exterior stairs and balconies are inspected and rebuilt where needed, with proper flashing and fasteners. The goal is a building that rents to students every year without needing a major overhaul after each lease cycle.

sections.h2: Shared systems and phasing in Raleigh multifamily
sections.body:
In most Raleigh duplexes and fourplexes, a few systems serve every unit: the roof, the main water line, the sewer lateral, the electrical service and sometimes a shared attic or crawlspace. Those items should come first, because they affect every tenant and can't be done well in pieces. We schedule shutoffs with advance notice through your property manager and complete shared work as quickly as possible.

Unit renovations can follow as leases end. Near NC State, the leasing cycle creates natural windows in summer when many units turn over at once, which makes it the obvious time for heavier interior work. In other parts of Raleigh, units come vacant on staggered schedules, so we renovate the first unit as a model, confirm the scope and pricing, then repeat it as each unit opens up. Throughout, we keep construction noise and dust controlled for occupied units and make sure fire separation and smoke alarms remain intact.

sections.h2: Adding units under Raleigh's missing middle rules
sections.body:
Raleigh's zoning changes in 2021 and 2022 allowed duplexes, triplexes, townhomes and backyard cottages in many residential districts where they were previously prohibited. For investors with larger lots inside or near the Beltline, converting a big older house into two units or adding a cottage behind an existing house can produce more value than a single-family flip.

The building code side of a conversion is where the cost lives. Separate units need fire-rated separation, independent egress, separate HVAC systems, smoke and carbon monoxide alarms and, usually, separate electrical meters. Water and sewer capacity may need to be upgraded, and City of Raleigh utility fees apply to new connections. During the Pre-Offer Rehab Review we look at whether the structure can be divided without major reframing, where the second entry and stair would go and what the utilities would require. That gives you real numbers to compare against a straight renovation before you buy.

faqs.q: When should I renovate a duplex near NC State?
faqs.a: Summer, between leases, is usually the most efficient window because many student units turn over at the same time and heavy interior work won't disrupt occupied units. We plan scopes in spring, order materials early and schedule trades so the work fits the gap between move-out and move-in. Shared exterior work like roofing and stairs can sometimes happen during the school year with tenants in place.

faqs.q: Do Raleigh duplex conversions need historic review?
faqs.a: Only if the property is in a Historic Overlay District such as Oakwood, Boylan Heights or Glenwood-Brooklyn, where exterior changes like a new entry, stair or addition require a Certificate of Appropriateness from the Raleigh Historic Development Commission. Interior changes aren't reviewed. Outside those districts, a conversion goes through zoning review and building permits with Development Services, and we account for both review steps in the schedule.

faqs.q: Can you renovate a Raleigh fourplex with tenants in place?
faqs.a: Yes. We handle shared systems first with scheduled shutoffs, then renovate units as they become vacant or on a schedule that works with your tenants. Your property manager receives the schedule and notices for any disruptive work. Phased renovations take longer, so we build that into the timeline and draw schedule from the beginning rather than adjusting midway, and tenants know what to expect before the first shutoff.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Raleigh, NC | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) certified contractor serving Raleigh and Wake County, NC: bids, consultant coordination and draws for Limited and Standard renovation loans.
fha-203k.intro: In a market where renovated houses get bid up quickly, the FHA 203(k) loan gives Raleigh buyers another path: buy the dated house nobody else wants and fold the renovation into the mortgage. Genstone Construction is an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor, and we work with Raleigh homebuyers, buyer's agents, renovation lenders and HUD consultants to produce the bids and documentation the program requires and then complete the work. Many of the houses that fit most often are the post-war ranches in Southeast Raleigh and around the Beltline, and the 1970s and 1980s houses in North Raleigh with siding, roof and mechanical problems that keep them from qualifying for a standard FHA loan.

sections.h2: Which 203(k) loan fits your Raleigh house
sections.body:
The Limited 203(k) covers non-structural repairs up to $75,000 and doesn't require a HUD consultant. In Raleigh, that typically handles a new roof, siding replacement, HVAC, a panel upgrade, a PEX repipe, new windows, a kitchen and baths, flooring and paint. Many North Raleigh houses with hardboard siding and aging systems fit within the Limited program, as long as the wall framing behind the siding turns out to be sound.

The Standard 203(k) is for structural work or larger projects. It has a $5,000 minimum repair amount, requires a HUD consultant who prepares the work write-up and inspects draws, and allows for things like foundation repair, moving walls, additions and major framing work. In Raleigh, Standard loans are common on the older houses near downtown where sills, joists or foundations need attention, and on ranches where buyers want to open up the floor plan. We'll give you our view of which program fits during the free Pre-Offer Rehab Review.

sections.h2: How Genstone works with Raleigh lenders and consultants
sections.body:
203(k) loans move at the pace of their paperwork. Lenders need a contractor bid that's itemized and consistent with the consultant's write-up on Standard loans, and they need proof of licensing and insurance. Genstone's estimators prepare detailed bids with labor and materials separated by line item, and we coordinate directly with the HUD consultant so the scope matches their work write-up before the loan goes to underwriting.

During construction, draws are requested as work is completed, and on Standard loans the consultant inspects before funds are released. City of Raleigh Development Services issues the permits and performs code inspections, and the final inspection needs to be complete before the last draw. We manage permits, inspections and lien waivers so the lender has everything at closeout. That structure lines up with how Genstone handles every project: no upfront payment, draws tied to finished work and final payment after the homeowner signs off.

A good 203(k) candidate has a purchase price that leaves room for the renovation and an as-improved value that supports the total loan amount. In Raleigh, that often describes ranches in Southeast Raleigh neighborhoods like Biltmore Hills and Worthdale, houses in East College Park and Longview Gardens, older homes in Garner, and North Raleigh split-levels with deferred maintenance.

Buyer's agents in Raleigh often turn to 203(k) when a standard FHA appraisal comes back with required repairs: a roof at the end of its life, peeling paint on a pre-1978 house, missing handrails, a non-working HVAC system or a damaged water heater. Instead of losing the deal, the buyer can finance the repairs. The program also covers one- to four-unit properties for owner-occupants, which makes it a route into a duplex near NC State or in an older neighborhood. Houses in Raleigh's Historic Overlay Districts can work too, though exterior changes need Historic Development Commission approval.

faqs.q: Do I need a HUD consultant for a Raleigh 203(k)?
faqs.a: Only on the Standard 203(k). The Limited 203(k) doesn't require one, which is part of why it's popular for non-structural updates on Raleigh houses. On Standard loans, the consultant prepares the work write-up, reviews the contractor bid and inspects work before each draw. We coordinate directly with the consultant your lender selects so the process stays on schedule and draw requests aren't held up by mismatched paperwork.

faqs.q: Can a 203(k) fix hardboard siding on a North Raleigh house?
faqs.a: Yes. Siding replacement is a non-structural repair that fits within the Limited 203(k) as long as the total stays within the program cap. If the swollen siding has let water into the wall framing and sheathing, structural repairs may push the project into the Standard program. We assess the wall condition during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review so the right loan type is chosen from the start.

faqs.q: Will a Raleigh 203(k) buyer have to move out during the renovation?
faqs.a: On larger projects, usually yes, because kitchens, baths and mechanical systems are torn out at the same time and the house isn't livable. The loan can include mortgage payments during the renovation period in some cases, so ask your lender. Smaller Limited projects sometimes allow the buyer to move in after key items are done. We'll give you a realistic schedule with the bid.

reo-renovation.title: REO and Bank-Owned Renovation in Raleigh, NC | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: REO and bank-owned property renovation in Raleigh and Wake County, NC for servicers, banks, funds and GSEs: secure, repair and document vacant houses.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Property Renovation in Raleigh
reo-renovation.intro: Raleigh's REO inventory is smaller than in some other North Carolina cities, but the properties that do come back to lenders tend to carry long lists of deferred maintenance, and Wake County buyers expect a market-ready house. Genstone Construction works with mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and other lenders, and we're a preferred contractor for Government-Sponsored Enterprises. We secure, repair and renovate bank-owned houses across the Raleigh area through a network of vetted, licensed local contractors, managed by a Genstone field manager who produces the documentation asset managers require: itemized bids, photo reports, permit records, inspection results and lien waivers from every trade. One contact, one file per address, and repairs scoped to the buyer the house is likely to attract.

sections.h2: Conditions common in vacant Raleigh houses
sections.body:
A vacant house in Raleigh faces the city's heat and humidity without the HVAC running, and mold growth inside closed-up rooms is one of the most frequent problems we find. Roof leaks under heavy tree cover make it worse, since clogged gutters and valleys overflow during summer storms and water runs into ceilings and walls. Crawlspaces under ranches and older houses collect moisture and attract pests, and wood floors above them can cup.

In winter, a house that wasn't winterized properly can freeze during a cold snap, especially when supply lines run through vented crawlspaces. Theft is common too: outdoor HVAC condensers, copper piping and appliances disappear from vacant houses, and broken windows or doors invite trespassers. Overgrown yards, piled debris and fallen limbs quickly attract code complaints. A Raleigh REO scope usually starts with securing the property and stopping water intrusion, then moves to mold remediation, system replacement and repairs that bring the house to marketable condition.

sections.h2: Raleigh code enforcement and REO permits
sections.body:
The City of Raleigh's Housing and Neighborhoods Department handles code enforcement for minimum housing standards, overgrown lots, debris and unsafe structures. Vacant properties draw complaints quickly in Raleigh's residential neighborhoods, and open code cases can complicate a sale or delay closing. We address cited violations as a first priority, document corrections with photos and coordinate re-inspection with the city.

Renovation work goes through City of Raleigh Development Services for permits and inspections, while properties outside the city limits fall under Wake County or the town where they're located. For REO clients, we keep all permit records, inspection results and lien waivers in the property file so they're available for buyers, title companies and lenders. Genstone Field Services, part of the Genstone Companies, can handle property preservation, inspections and code compliance before and after renovation, which keeps the property's documentation consistent from start to finish. That continuity helps when a buyer's lender asks for proof that a cited violation was actually corrected.

sections.h2: Repair-to-sell or full renovation in Raleigh
sections.body:
Asset managers in Raleigh have to decide how much to invest in a bank-owned house before listing it. A repair-to-market scope brings the property to a condition that qualifies for FHA or conventional financing: working HVAC, a sound roof, functional plumbing and electrical, safety items like handrails and smoke alarms, and repair of peeling paint on pre-1978 houses. That widens the buyer pool beyond cash investors.

A fuller renovation makes sense in neighborhoods where owner-occupant demand is strong and buyers compare the property to renovated listings, which describes much of Wake County. Updated kitchens, baths and flooring can significantly change the price a house commands in those areas. We price both options when the decision isn't obvious, with line items and photos in the format the client requires, so the asset manager can compare expected recovery under each scenario. Inside the Beltline, a bank-owned house may also attract builders as a teardown, which is worth considering before committing to any renovation.

faqs.q: Does Genstone work for mortgage servicers in Raleigh?
faqs.a: Yes. Our clients include mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and other lenders, and we are a preferred contractor for Government-Sponsored Enterprises. In the Raleigh area we provide bids in the formats servicers require, coordinate licensed local trades and deliver photo documentation, permit records and lien waivers for every property. Each job has a designated field manager who serves as the single point of contact.

faqs.q: How quickly can you secure a vacant Raleigh property?
faqs.a: Securing a property, boarding openings, changing locks and stopping active water intrusion are treated as first priorities on every Raleigh REO. Genstone Field Services handles property preservation work for clients who need it, and we coordinate those tasks with any renovation scope so the property doesn't deteriorate further while bids are being reviewed. Exact timing depends on the property and access.

faqs.q: What happens with mold in a Raleigh bank-owned house?
faqs.a: We identify the source of moisture first, whether a roof leak, plumbing failure, condensation from a disabled HVAC system or crawlspace moisture. Then affected materials are removed, the cause is corrected and the area is documented before and after for the asset manager. Larger mold problems are handled by a licensed remediation specialist coordinated within the same project, so the asset manager isn't managing a second vendor.
